title: Ezekiel 36:22–32
context: The Lord GOD tells the house of Israel that he will act not for their sake but for his holy name, profaned among the nations (36:22–23). He will gather them, sprinkle clean water on them, give them a new heart and a new spirit, take away the stony heart, give a heart of flesh, and put his Spirit within them so that they walk in his statutes (36:24–27). The covenant formula follows: “You will be my people, and I will be your God” (36:28), along with plenty in place of famine (36:29–30). Israel will remember its ways with shame (36:31–32). The promise closely parallels Ezekiel 11:17–20 and is often read alongside Jeremiah 31:33; these are named here without merging them. On how God’s gift of a new heart relates to human response, the boxes at Deuteronomy 5:29 and 10:16 treat this; see also Deuteronomy 30:6. Some Christian readers also hear an echo in John 3:5, a link they hold with varying confidence. The phrase “not for your sake” concerns the LORD’s name among the nations, and both traditions read it as shared ground.

verses.text: “Therefore tell the house of Israel, ‘The Lord GOD says: “I don’t do this for your sake, house of Israel, but for my holy name, which you have profaned among the nations where you went.
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD says he acts not for Israel’s sake but for his holy name. Arminian readers see the restoration as wholly gracious, not earned by Israel, and aimed at making God known.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see grace rooted in God’s own purposes, not in Israel’s merit. Shared ground: both traditions read not for your sake as concerning the LORD’s name among the nations, and they agree that this grace leaves no room for boasting.

verses.text: I will sanctify my great name, which has been profaned among the nations, which you have profaned among them. Then the nations will know that I am the LORD,” says the Lord GOD, “when I am proven holy in you before their eyes.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will sanctify his great name, and the nations will know him when he is proven holy in Israel before their eyes. Arminian readers see God’s restoring work as a witness to all peoples.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear in proven holy in you the thought that God displays his holiness through what he does for and in his people. Both traditions read the verse as linking Israel’s restoration with the knowledge of the LORD among the nations.

verses.text: “ ‘ “For I will take you from among the nations and gather you out of all the countries, and will bring you into your own land.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will take them from the nations, gather them, and bring them into their own land. Arminian readers see the promised return as the first act of restoration, reversing the scattering of 36:19.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s initiative in the gathering, compare Ezekiel 11:17 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a promise of return from exile, which also opens onto the inner renewal that follows.

verses.text: I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean. I will cleanse you from all your filthiness and from all your idols.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will sprinkle clean water on them and cleanse them from filthiness and idols. Arminian readers see cleansing as God’s gracious provision, which his people receive and live out.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image of purification as God’s own act on behalf of his people. Both traditions read the verse in light of purification rites, and some Christian readers in both hear a later echo, compare John 3:5 by reference, held with varying confidence.

verses.text: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will give a new heart and new spirit, removing the stony heart and giving a heart of flesh. Arminian readers see a promised new heart given by grace, a covenant promise that enables response and may be resisted; they often speak of prevenient grace here. Compare Ezekiel 11:19 and Jeremiah 31:33, named without merging the settings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign renewal of the heart, an effectual new heart that causes obedience. The boxes at Deuteronomy 5:29 and 10:16 treat this; see also Deuteronomy 30:6.

verses.text: I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes. You will keep my ordinances and do them.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will put his Spirit within them and cause them to walk in his statutes. Arminian readers see the Spirit’s work enabling obedience, a gracious gift that brings people into active faithfulness and does not remove the possibility of resistance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see cause you to walk as the Spirit effectively producing obedience. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as God’s Spirit making new life possible. The boxes at Deuteronomy 5:29 and 10:16 treat how they differ; see also Deuteronomy 30:6.

verses.text: You will dwell in the land that I gave to your fathers. You will be my people, and I will be your God.
verses.arminianNotes: They will dwell in the land given to their fathers, and be his people while he is their God. Arminian readers see the covenant relationship restored, the goal of God’s renewing work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the covenant formula, compare Ezekiel 11:20 and Jeremiah 31:33 by reference, as the heart of the promise. Both traditions read the verse as relationship renewed, with land and people restored together.

verses.text: I will save you from all your uncleanness. I will call for the grain and will multiply it, and lay no famine on you.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will save them from uncleanness, call for grain, and lay no famine on them. Arminian readers see salvation reaching body and land as well as heart, a full restoration.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s provision as the fruit of his covenant faithfulness. Shared ground: both traditions read the promise as reversing the famines of judgment described in chapters 4–7.

verses.text: I will multiply the fruit of the tree and the increase of the field, that you may receive no more the reproach of famine among the nations.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will multiply fruit and harvest so they no longer bear the reproach of famine among the nations. Arminian readers see blessing that removes shame, so that God’s people are no longer mocked.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the harvests as a public sign of covenant blessing, ending the scorn that famine had brought. Both traditions read the verse as tying material plenty to the vindication of the LORD’s name among the peoples.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Then you will remember your evil ways, and your deeds that were not good; and you will loathe yourselves in your own sight for your iniquities and for your abominations.
verses.arminianNotes: Then they will remember their evil ways and loathe themselves for their iniquities. Arminian readers see grace producing repentance, as kindness leads people to see their sin clearly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see renewed hearts recognizing the depth of past sin, compare 6:9 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions read the remembrance as following God’s gift, a humble response to grace received.

verses.text: I don’t do this for your sake,” says the Lord GOD. “Let it be known to you. Be ashamed and confounded for your ways, house of Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD repeats that he acts for a reason beyond Israel’s deserving, and calls them to be ashamed of their ways. Arminian readers see the repetition guarding against pride, so that Israel claims no credit for restoration.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the restatement of 36:22 underlining grace and God’s concern for his name. Both traditions read the verse as shared ground on humility before God, where shame over the past and gratitude for mercy belong together.
